subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 62-year-old fair-skinned man notices a slow-growing, waxy, pink 'pearly' nodule on his nose. It has prominent telangiectasias, rolled borders, and a central area of crusting and ulceration. He has no palpable lymph nodes, and the lesion has never metastasized.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common skin cancer and arises in sun-exposed areas such as the face. It appears as a waxy, pink, pearly nodule with telangiectasias, rolled borders, and central crusting or ulceration. It is locally invasive but rarely metastasizes, which fits this patient's lack of nodal disease. BCC is more common above the upper lip.

explanation_incorrect.A: SCC is the second most common skin cancer and typically presents as an ulcerative red lesion with keratin pearls, often on the lower lip, ears, or hands; it is associated with immunosuppression and chronic wounds rather than a pearly nodule.
explanation_incorrect.C: Melanoma is a pigmented tumor with ABCDE features and a significant risk of metastasis; it lacks the pearly, telangiectatic, rolled-border appearance described here.
explanation_incorrect.D: Actinic keratosis is a small, rough, erythematous or brownish premalignant papule caused by sun exposure, not a nodular ulcerated lesion.
explanation_incorrect.E: Lentigo maligna is a melanoma in situ seen on sun-exposed skin of older patients as a flat, irregularly pigmented macule, not a pearly nodule.

educationalObjective: A waxy pearly nodule with telangiectasias and rolled borders on the sun-exposed face is the classic presentation of basal cell carcinoma, which rarely metastasizes.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 54-year-old renal transplant recipient develops a nonhealing, ulcerative red lesion on his lower lip and another on the dorsum of his hand. Biopsy shows malignant keratinocytes forming keratin pearls. The lesions are locally invasive, and one is associated with enlarged cervical lymph nodes, but distant disease is absent.
question: Which of the following best characterizes the tumor in this patient?

options.text: Basal cell carcinoma that frequently metastasizes to distant sites
Malignant melanoma that is S-100 negative
Actinic keratosis with a low risk of malignant transformation
Squamous cell carcinoma that may spread to lymph nodes but rarely metastasizes distantly
Superficial basal cell carcinoma with a high rate of nodal spread

explanation_correct: SCC is the second most common skin cancer and is associated with immunosuppression, chronic nonhealing wounds, and arsenic exposure. It appears as an ulcerative red lesion with keratin pearls on histopathology, favors the face, lower lip, ears, and hands (more common below the lower lip), and is locally invasive. It may spread to lymph nodes but rarely metastasizes distantly.

explanation_incorrect.A: BCC rarely metastasizes at all, is not strongly associated with immunosuppression, and shows palisading basal cells rather than keratin pearls.
explanation_incorrect.B: Melanoma is S-100 positive, arises from melanocytes, and would not produce keratin pearls; it also metastasizes much more readily than this tumor.
explanation_incorrect.C: Actinic keratosis is a premalignant sun-induced lesion, not an invasive cancer with keratin pearls and nodal spread.
explanation_incorrect.E: Superficial BCC appears as a scaling plaque and, like other BCCs, rarely spreads to nodes; it does not form keratin pearls.

educationalObjective: Squamous cell carcinoma shows keratin pearls, arises in immunosuppression and chronic wounds, and may spread to nodes but rarely metastasizes distantly.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 70-year-old man has had a chronic, nonhealing burn scar on his leg for 25 years. Over the past year the scar transformed into an ulcerative, red, raised lesion. Biopsy reveals well-differentiated malignant keratinocytes with keratin pearls.
question: Which of the following best describes this lesion?

options.text: Squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic wound (Marjolin ulcer)
Basal cell carcinoma arising de novo on the lower leg

explanation_correct: A Marjolin ulcer is squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic wound or scar, usually developing more than 20 years after the original insult. This patient's long-standing burn scar with malignant transformation and keratin pearls fits SCC. SCC is associated with chronic nonhealing wounds, immunosuppression, and arsenic exposure.

explanation_incorrect.B: BCC does not typically arise in chronic scars, rarely metastasizes, and shows palisading basal cells rather than keratin pearls.
explanation_incorrect.C: Acral lentiginous melanoma occurs on palms, soles, or nail beds, has the highest prevalence in darker-skinned individuals, and is not associated with chronic scars or keratin pearls.
explanation_incorrect.D: Actinic keratosis is a small, rough, sun-induced premalignant papule; it does not arise as a large ulcerating lesion within a decades-old scar.
explanation_incorrect.E: Lentigo maligna melanoma arises on sun-exposed skin as a flat pigmented lesion, not within a chronic burn scar, and would not form keratin pearls.

educationalObjective: A Marjolin ulcer is squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic wound or scar, typically more than 20 years after the initial injury.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 66-year-old farmer with a long history of sun exposure has several small, rough, erythematous and brownish papules on his forehead and the backs of his hands. A biopsy would show partial-thickness epithelial dysplasia. He is counseled that these lesions have malignant potential.
question: Which of the following best describes these lesions?

options.text: Benign seborrheic keratoses with no malignant potential
Basal cell carcinomas that rarely metastasize
Premalignant lesions whose risk of progression to squamous cell carcinoma is proportional to the degree of epithelial dysplasia
Melanomas in situ with a high risk of nodal metastasis
Fully invasive squamous cell carcinomas producing keratin pearls

explanation_correct: Actinic keratoses are premalignant lesions caused by sun exposure, appearing as small, rough, erythematous or brownish papules or plaques. The risk of progression to squamous cell carcinoma is proportional to the degree of epithelial dysplasia. They are a precursor lesion rather than invasive cancer.

explanation_incorrect.A: Seborrheic keratoses are benign, stuck-on plaques without dysplasia; the lesions described are sun-induced premalignant keratoses.
explanation_incorrect.B: BCC is a malignant tumor with palisading basal cells and a pearly nodule appearance, not a rough premalignant papule with dysplasia.
explanation_incorrect.D: Melanoma in situ is a melanocytic lesion with S-100 positivity and ABCDE features, not a rough keratinocytic papule related to actinic damage.
explanation_incorrect.E: Invasive SCC would show full-thickness malignant keratinocytes and keratin pearls, not the partial-thickness dysplasia of a premalignant keratosis.

educationalObjective: Actinic keratoses are sun-induced premalignant lesions whose risk of becoming squamous cell carcinoma parallels their degree of epithelial dysplasia.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 45-year-old woman has a pigmented skin lesion on her back that was excised. Histopathology confirms malignant melanoma. The pathology report emphasizes measurement of the vertical thickness of the tumor from the granular layer to the deepest point of invasion. The oncologist uses this measurement to estimate her risk of metastasis.
question: Which of the following tumor features is most directly correlated with the risk of metastasis in melanoma?

options.text: The diameter of the lesion being greater than 6 mm
The presence of surrounding dysplastic nevi

explanation_correct: Breslow thickness measures the vertical depth of the melanoma from the granular layer of the epidermis to the deepest point of tumor invasion. Depth of invasion correlates directly with the risk of metastasis and is the key prognostic factor used to guide staging and wide excision margins. S-100 is a diagnostic tumor marker, not a measure of metastatic risk.

explanation_incorrect.A: Diameter greater than 6 mm is one of the ABCDE warning signs that raises suspicion for melanoma, but it is not the measurement that correlates most directly with metastatic risk.
explanation_incorrect.B: S-100 is an immunohistochemical tumor marker helpful in identifying melanoma, not a quantitative predictor of metastasis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Dysplastic nevi are associated with increased melanoma risk, but their presence does not determine the metastatic potential of an existing tumor.
explanation_incorrect.D: Lighter skin tone is a risk factor for developing melanoma, not a determinant of metastasis for a tumor already excised.

educationalObjective: Breslow thickness (depth of invasion) of a melanoma correlates with metastatic risk and guides staging and treatment.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 38-year-old fair-skinned man with many dysplastic nevi notices that a mole on his shoulder has become asymmetric, with an irregular border, variegated colors, and a diameter of 8 mm. It has also changed in size and shape over the past 6 months.
question: Which of the following features in this patient's lesion is most suggestive of melanoma?

options.text: A stable, symmetric, uniformly colored lesion smaller than 6 mm
A pearly nodule with telangiectasias on the face
Evolution over time with asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, and diameter >6 mm
A small rough erythematous papule on the dorsum of the hand
A waxy plaque with rolled borders and central ulceration on the nose

explanation_correct: Melanoma is suggested by the ABCDEs: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter greater than 6 mm, and Evolution over time. This lesion has all of these features. Melanoma is associated with dysplastic nevi and lighter skin tones and is often driven by activating BRAF mutations.

explanation_incorrect.A: A small, symmetric, uniformly colored stable lesion is a benign nevus and lacks the ABCDE warning features.
explanation_incorrect.B: A pearly nodule with telangiectasias on the face is basal cell carcinoma, not melanoma.
explanation_incorrect.D: A small rough erythematous papule on a sun-exposed hand suggests actinic keratosis, a premalignant keratinocytic lesion.
explanation_incorrect.E: A waxy plaque with rolled borders and central ulceration is basal cell carcinoma; it is not a pigmented melanocytic lesion.

educationalObjective: The ABCDE criteria (asymmetry, border irregularity, color variation, diameter >6 mm, evolution) identify suspicious melanocytic lesions.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 60-year-old Black patient develops a slowly enlarging, irregularly pigmented macule on the plantar surface of the foot. It has been present for over a year and is not related to sun exposure. Biopsy confirms melanoma.
question: Which histologic subtype of melanoma has the highest prevalence in individuals with darker skin tones?
explanation_correct: Acral lentiginous melanoma has the highest prevalence in people with darker skin tones and arises on acral sites such as the palms, soles, and nail beds, often independent of sun exposure. The other recognized types are superficial spreading, nodular, and lentigo maligna melanoma.

explanation_incorrect.A: Superficial spreading melanoma is the most common subtype overall but is not the one with the highest prevalence in darker-skinned individuals and typically arises on sun-exposed skin.
explanation_incorrect.C: Lentigo maligna melanoma arises on chronically sun-exposed skin of older patients as a flat pigmented lesion, not on the soles.
explanation_incorrect.D: Nodular melanoma is a vertically growing, often symmetric dome-shaped tumor and is not specifically associated with darker skin or acral sites.
explanation_incorrect.E: Amelanotic melanoma lacks pigment and is a descriptive variant, not one of the four main subtypes; it does not specifically predominate in darker skin.

educationalObjective: Acral lentiginous melanoma predominates in darker-skinned individuals and arises on palms, soles, and nail beds.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 52-year-old woman has metastatic melanoma. Molecular testing of the tumor reveals an activating mutation in BRAF kinase. Her oncologist discusses targeted therapy with a BRAF inhibitor as well as immunotherapy.
question: Which of the following pairs a melanoma-associated molecular finding with an appropriate targeted therapy?
explanation_correct: Melanoma is often driven by activating mutations in BRAF kinase. Patients with these mutations can be treated with BRAF inhibitors such as vemurafenib. Advanced melanoma is also treated with immunotherapy such as ipilimumab, but ipilimumab is not a BRAF-targeted therapy; primary treatment is wide excision.

explanation_incorrect.A: Ipilimumab is an immunotherapy (immune checkpoint inhibitor), not a targeted therapy for BRAF; the targeted drug for an activating BRAF mutation is vemurafenib.
explanation_incorrect.B: S-100 is a diagnostic tumor marker, not a therapeutic target, and is not treated with vemurafenib.
explanation_incorrect.C: Melanoma is classically associated with activating BRAF mutations, not KRAS; vemurafenib targets BRAF.
explanation_incorrect.E: Melanoma involves activating (not loss of) BRAF mutations, and ipilimumab is immunotherapy rather than a replacement for lost BRAF function.

educationalObjective: Melanoma with an activating BRAF mutation can be treated with the BRAF inhibitor vemurafenib; ipilimumab is immunotherapy.
